Article Title: In 2024, Palau removed invasive rats from Ulong Island; one year later, fish biomass rose 183% and leaf nitrogen increased about 80% at one reef site
Article Text:
Data from Ulong Island, Koror Republic of Palau shows that seabirds are returning (Representational AP photo)

First signs of recovery

The process is supporting reef ecosystems and increasing fish populations.

Nutrients and fish populations

A seabird flying over the coast of Palau (Greg Metro photography)

Removing rats

The return of seabirds to a small island in Palau has brought an unexpected benefit. Just one year after invasive rats were removed from Ulong Island, researchers have found that nearby coral reefs are also beginning to recover.The study is the first experimental research to show that when seabirds return after invasive rodents are removed, they help move nutrients from land into the sea. The process is already supporting reef ecosystems and increasing fish populations much sooner than expected.According to Island Conservation, the research was carried out on Ulong Island in the Republic of Palau, an island nation in Western Pacific Ocean, as part of the Island-Ocean Connection Challenge (IOCC). Scientists from Island Conservation and the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California San Diego monitored the island before and after the rat removal.They tracked changes in seabirds, nutrients, reef fish and other marine life while comparing the results with a nearby island, Ngeruktabel, where invasive rats remain.The findings suggest that restoring island ecosystems can also improve the health of nearby oceans and shows how closely land and sea are connected.Researchers say seeing measurable changes in such a short time is surprising. "Seeing measurable ecological change just one year after restoration is extraordinary. It demonstrates the power of local leadership and science working together to heal island ecosystems from ridge to reef," said Coral Wolf, Conservation Impact Program Manager at Island Conservation.One of the clearest signs of recovery was the return of birds. The endangered Palau Ground Dove was detected more often after the restoration work. Seabird activity also increased massively. Calls of Bridled Terns rose by 286%, while Brown Noddy and White Tern calls increased by around 50% compared with the nearby control island, where rats had not been removed.Scientists say seabirds play an important role because they feed in the ocean but nest on land. Their droppings, known as guano, carry nutrients from the sea onto islands. Rain then washes some of these nutrients into nearby coastal waters, helping support marine life.The researchers also found changes in the island's soil and surrounding waters. Decline in nitrogen signatures happened more slowly on Ulong than at other sites. According to the researchers, this matches what would be expected if seabird guano was beginning to add nutrients back into the soil and nearby marine environment.Fish populations also responded earlier than expected. There has been significant increase in fish biomass around Ulong, suggesting that the returning nutrients were already supporting reef productivity.One monitoring site showed particularly strong changes. Researchers recorded increases in several seabird species, an approximately 80% rise in leaf nitrogen and a 183% increase in total fish biomass.Although these changes were seen at only one monitoring site, scientists say the speed of recovery was much faster than they had predicted.Nathaniel Hanna Holloway, a marine ecologist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, says the findings provide direct evidence of how restoring islands can benefit nearby reefs."These early signals from Ulong show how quickly ecosystems can rebound when stressors are removed. For the first time in Palau, we're seeing measurable evidence of seabird-driven nutrient flow returning to the land and sea. It's powerful proof that terrestrial action spills over into benefits for surrounding reef communities, which people rely on for their livelihoods," Holloway said.Invasive rats are one of the biggest threats to island ecosystems around the world. They prey on bird eggs and chicks, preventing many seabird populations from recovering.When seabird numbers fall, fewer nutrients are carried from the ocean onto islands. This weakens not only land ecosystems but can also reduce the nutrients reaching nearby coastal waters.Scientists say this connection between land restoration and marine recovery had previously been suggested by observational studies. However, the Ulong project is the first experimental study to demonstrate the process using before-and-after monitoring alongside a comparison island.
Article Summary: Invasive rats were removed from Ulong Island, Republic of Palau, one year ago. Scientists tracked changes in seabirds, nutrients, reef fish and other marine life. Seabirds play an important role because they feed in the ocean but nest on land. Their droppings carry nutrients from the sea onto islands. Rain washes some of these nutrients into nearby coastal waters.

Article Title: Britain is dropping 20 concrete reef cubes and 44 tons of scallop shells into the sea in the hope to bring back its native oysters who have reduced by 95% since 1800s
Article Text:
Twenty cubes for a new seabed

A special place for the oysters

Fish, crabs, shrimp, and many small invertebrates can use its gaps for food and shelter, which is why restoring oysters is about much more than restoring one shellfish species.

95% collapse changes European seas

Why native oysters are important

While one might assume that lowering huge white blocks of concrete into the sea was an attempt at dumping construction waste offshore, in Britain's North Sea it is a conservation effort. The country is dumping 20 carefully designed structures into the deep waters to restore the population of the European native oyster, Ostrea edulis, along England's northeast coast.The 2025 operation combined the reef cubes with 4,000 mature oysters, more than 35,000 juveniles and about 44 US tons of repurposed scallop shells. In the United Kingdom, the number of native oysters has fallen by more than 95% since the 1800s and the project is studying whether sturdy engineering can give a lost ecosystem the foothold it needs to rebuild, as per a report by econews.Each reef cube weighs about 6.6 US tons, meaning the 20 structures together weigh around 132 tons. They have been created from Marine Crete, a seawater-resistant material that the project team describes as a carbon-neutral alternative to ordinary concrete.They have been designed with ridges, textured surfaces and large openings to give oysters a place to attach while creating hiding spaces for fish, lobsters, sponges and other marine life.Volunteers attached 4,000 adult oysters to the cubes with specialist reef adhesive. The team also lowered juvenile oysters already growing on shells, and recycled scallop shells known as "clutch" onto a site about 1.1 miles offshore.The new cube designs reflect lessons learned from an earlier deployment in 2023. Conservationists placed 10,000 mature oysters on roughly 827 US tons of shell and stone off Whitburn, but Storm Babet and other severe weather conditions moved some of that loose reef material soon afterwards. Monitoring has still found oysters surviving and establishing in the area. Even so, the exposed North Sea coastline is a rougher testing ground than a sheltered bay or estuary, where currents and waves are less likely to scatter a young reef. That is why the heavy cubes now act as anchors.As for the oysters, before they went to sea, 90 volunteers cleaned and scrubbed them at North Shields Fish Quay. The work reduced the risk of unintentionally moving other organisms into the restoration site. Nearly 100 more volunteers then helped attach oysters to the reef cubes. A survey vessel carried the structures, juveniles, and shell material offshore before carefully lowering everything onto the seabed.Young oysters begin life as tiny larvae moving through the water. When they are ready to settle, they need a firm surface, often an older oyster shell, where they can attach and continue growing.But with a vanished reef, this single requirement becomes a major obstacle. A flat or shifting seabed offers fewer safe places to settle, while a layer of shells can work like the foundation of a crowded underwater neighbourhood. As generations grow on top of earlier shells, the reef becomes three-dimensional. Fish, crabs, shrimp, and many small invertebrates can use its gaps for food and shelter, which is why restoring oysters is about much more than restoring one shellfish species.One of the major factors that played a big role in the loss of native oysters was overharvesting them faster than they could recover. Then pollution, disease and habitat destruction added more pressure to it. Native reefs disappeared from this part of northeast England more than a century ago, and oysters are now locally extinct or functionally absent across much of their former range.A wider assessment led by ZSL and the University of Edinburgh found that Europe's native oyster reef ecosystem met the criteria for being classified as "collapsed." Historical evidence indicated that these reefs once covered more than 4.2 million acres across Europe, creating complex habitats that looked very different from today’s mostly flat seabeds.Native oysters are filter feeders, meaning they draw in seawater and remove suspended material as they feed. As per the Zoological Society of London, one adult can filter around 53 gallons in a day, although the total effect depends on oyster numbers and local conditions. This filtration helps improve water clarity and cycle nutrients.While it is not a substitute for controlling sewage, pollution or runoff, a healthy reef can become part of the sea's natural maintenance system. “They may be small, but oysters can play an important role in keeping our seas clean and healthy,” said Celine Gamble, the Wild Oysters Project manager, as per econews.Now, the project awaits success which would mean survival, reproduction, new juvenile settlement and a gradual return of a self-sustaining reef that supports a wider community of marine species. Researchers will also be watching whether the structures attract fish and invertebrates, improve habitat complexity, and remain stable through winter storms.
Article Summary: Britain is dumping 20 carefully designed structures into the deep waters to restore the population of the European native oyster, Ostrea edulis. The number of native oysters has fallen by more than 95% since the 1800s and the project is studying whether sturdy engineering can give a lost ecosystem the foothold it needs to rebuild.

Article Title: Four killed in helicopter crash in Rio de Janeiro
Article Text:
Emergency personnel stand near the site where, according to fire department officials, a helicopter crashed killing the pilot and 3 tourists. (AP Photo)

Four people were killed after a helicopter crashed in Rio de Janeiro's Tijuca National Park on Saturday, Brazilian fire officials said. Brazilian media reported that three of those killed were Colombian tourists.The helicopter crashed in a mountainous part of the national park, an area covered by dense vegetation and difficult to access. Firefighters said the pilot and three women "burned to death".Images released by the fire department showed the charred wreckage of the helicopter smoking on a steep hillside.A police source told AFP that the victims had not yet been officially identified. However, local media reports said the three female passengers were Colombian nationals, while Brazilian news site G1 reported that they belonged to the same family.The crash occurred near Vista Chinesa, a replica of a Chinese pagoda located at a high altitude and known for its panoramic views of Rio de Janeiro from within the forest. The landmark also featured in the 2011 animated film "Rio".The latest crash comes less than two months after another helicopter accident in Rio de Janeiro. In June, two helicopters collided over the city, killing six people, including American singer Oliver Tree and Argentine YouTuber Gaspar Prim.Helicopter tours are popular among tourists visiting Rio, offering aerial views of the city's landmarks and coastline.Following Saturday's crash, Rio de Janeiro Mayor Eduardo Cavaliere said on X that he had asked Brazil's National Civil Aviation Agency to immediately step up monitoring to ensure the safety of helicopter flights.
Article Summary: Four people killed after helicopter crashes in Rio de Janeiro's Tijuca National Park. Firefighters said the pilot and three women "burned to death" Brazilian media reported that three of those killed were Colombian tourists. The crash occurred near Vista Chinesa, a replica of a Chinese pagoda.

Article Title: Defence: Pentagon asks defence firms to ramp up weapons production as Iran war drains stockpile: Report
Article Text:
After heavy depletion of missile stocks, Pentagon asks defence firms to ramp up weapons production. Donald Trump, Pete Hegseth (AP image)

Why is the Pentagon asking for faster production?

How badly have US missile stocks been depleted?

THAAD: One of the biggest concerns

Patriot: Stocks also sharply lower

What about Tomahawk and other offensive missiles?

Why can't defence companies simply make more missiles?

What exactly does the Pentagon want from defence firms?

How long could rebuilding US stocks take?

THAAD: CSIS estimates that replacing the interceptors used during the conflict could take until the end of 2029.

Patriot: Rebuilding more than 1,000 Patriot interceptors used during the conflict could take until around the middle of 2029, according to the CSIS assessment.

Tomahawk: Existing production schedules could leave US inventories below pre-war levels until late 2030.

SM-3 and SM-6: Production and delivery could take several years, with CSIS estimating lead times of roughly 36 to 39 months after funding approval.

JASSM: The recovery could be faster because the US had larger stocks and production was already relatively high before the war.

PrSM: Since the Precision Strike Missile is a newer system and the pre-war inventory was relatively small, rebuilding stocks could take considerably less time.

Why are Patriot and THAAD particularly important?

Why is China part of the Pentagon's concern?

Pentagon says stocks are sufficient for current war

What does this mean for America's defence industry?

The funding battle in Congress

The US Pentagon has asked defence companies to urgently accelerate weapons production and deliveries as Washington faces growing pressure to replenish critical munitions depleted during the war with Iran, according to a memo obtained by The Washington Post.The request comes amid reports that stocks of key air-defence interceptors, including THAAD and Patriot, have fallen sharply from pre-war levels.Deputy defence secretary Steve Feinberg wrote to defence industry leaders on Wednesday, giving them 21 days to submit plans for "significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities"."Years-long development timelines are unacceptable," Feinberg wrote. "We must dramatically accelerate our program schedules and expand our production capacity now."The Pentagon said the push to increase production is part of a broader effort to rebuild the US defence industrial base and is not solely a response to the five-month-old conflict with Iran.Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell confirmed that Feinberg's memo was "real", saying the department was focused on accelerating munitions acquisitions to provide "the weapons our warfighters need at the pace the threat demands."At the same time, US officials have rejected suggestions that the military has run out of weapons needed for current operations. Jarred Conley, principal deputy director at the Defence Department's Defence Innovation Unit, told Al Jazeera that US stocks remained adequate."We have sufficient munitions for the task at hand. The department has everything it needs today to execute a war," Conley said.The conflicting assessments reflect the central issue facing Washington: the US may still have enough weapons to conduct current operations, but replacing the large quantities of sophisticated missiles already used could take years.The latest directive comes after months of intensive military operations that have placed pressure on US stocks of precision weapons and missile interceptors.The US has relied heavily on systems such as Patriot and Terminal High Altitude Area Defence, or THAAD, to protect American forces and allies from Iranian missiles and drones. At the same time, American forces have used long-range strike weapons during offensive operations.The concern is not simply whether the US has enough weapons for the immediate conflict. Defence planners are also looking at whether Washington would have sufficient stocks if another major crisis erupted soon after the Iran war.A recent analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, or CSIS, warned that depleted inventories could force the US and its Middle Eastern allies to take greater risks in defending against incoming missiles and drones.For example, forces could be forced to use fewer interceptors against some incoming threats in order to conserve supplies, increasing the possibility that a missile or drone could get through.The Pentagon's latest directive is therefore aimed at tackling both the immediate replenishment problem and the longer-term production capacity of the US defence industry.The exact size of America's current weapons inventories is classified. However, CSIS has estimated the depletion of some of the most important missile-defence systems using procurement data, production figures and publicly available information.The Terminal High Altitude Area Defence system is designed to intercept ballistic missiles at high altitudes before they reach their targets.CSIS estimated that the US had about 452 THAAD interceptors before the war. The stockpile fell to between 232 and 262 by the start of the April ceasefire.Some replenishment subsequently took place, taking the estimated inventory to between 234 and 278 interceptors. Even so, the stockpile remains at least 38% below its pre-war level, according to the CSIS figures cited by AP.A separate CNN report cited sources as saying the US had used nearly four-fifths of its THAAD inventory compared with pre-war levels. The differing estimates reflect the difficulty of assessing current stocks because official figures are not publicly disclosed.The key point is that THAAD inventories have come under heavy pressure and rebuilding them will take time.The Patriot system is another crucial part of the US missile-defence network.CSIS estimated that the US had around 2,330 Patriot interceptors before the war. That number fell to about 1,030 by the April ceasefire.Following subsequent fighting, the estimated stockpile dropped further to between 759 and 827 interceptors. That represents a decline of at least 65% from the pre-war level, according to the CSIS assessment cited by AP.Patriot systems are particularly important because they are not required only by the US military. American allies, including Ukraine and several Middle Eastern countries, also depend on the system. This means Washington faces competing demands for a limited number of interceptors.The pressure extends beyond missile-defence systems.The US has also used large numbers of long-range precision weapons during the conflict with Iran. Among them are Tomahawk cruise missiles, which are launched from ships and submarines and are designed to strike targets deep inside enemy territory.According to the CSIS assessment cited in the supplied material, the US fired more than 1,000 Tomahawks during the Iran war.The problem is that production had historically been relatively slow. Between fiscal years 2015 and 2026, US procurement averaged roughly 86 Tomahawks a year.That means even a major increase in annual orders cannot immediately replace thousands of missiles used during a prolonged conflict.The Pentagon has requested hundreds of additional Tomahawks as part of its effort to rebuild stocks, but delivery timelines remain long.CSIS has estimated that US Tomahawk inventories could take until late 2030 to return to pre-war levels under existing delivery schedules.This is one of the biggest challenges facing the Pentagon. Modern missiles are not mass-produced like conventional consumer goods. They require specialised components, advanced electronics, guidance systems, rocket motors, seekers, specialised metals and highly trained workers.Many components are manufactured by a limited number of suppliers. Increasing production therefore requires more than simply giving a defence company a larger order.Companies may need to establish new production lines, purchase machinery, expand factories, hire and train workers and secure additional suppliers.Congress must also approve funding before many of these programmes can move forward.This creates a gap between the Pentagon deciding that it needs more weapons and those weapons actually reaching military inventories.Some advanced missile systems can take several years from funding approval to delivery.That is why Feinberg's demand for companies to submit plans within 21 days is aimed not only at increasing production but also at shortening the time required to deliver weapons.Feinberg's memo asks companies to identify ways to accelerate production and delivery of critical capabilities.The Pentagon wants industry to examine where existing production schedules can be shortened and where manufacturing capacity can be expanded.The department is also looking at bottlenecks in the supply chain.The broader effort includes increasing production of components used in Patriot and THAAD interceptors, including rocket motors and other critical parts.The Pentagon has already entered into agreements with major defence companies to expand production capacity.According to the supplied material, agreements with Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman worth more than $3 billion are intended to expand production of components used in Patriot PAC-3 and THAAD systems.The Pentagon has said the broader initiative is designed to triple Patriot production capacity and quadruple THAAD production, while also adding another supplier for PAC-3 rocket motors.The aim is to ensure that a shortage of one component does not slow production of an entire missile system.The answer varies from one weapon system to another.The differences show why the Pentagon is focusing on production capacity rather than simply placing larger orders.Patriot and THAAD perform different roles but form a critical part of the US and allied missile-defence network.Patriot interceptors are used to engage incoming missiles at lower altitudes and have become one of the most sought-after air-defence systems in the world.THAAD operates at a higher altitude and is designed primarily to intercept ballistic missiles during the terminal phase of their flight.Both systems became particularly important during Iranian missile attacks against US forces and regional allies.A reduction in their inventories could limit the number of interceptors available for future attacks.The problem is made more complicated by demand from allies. Ukraine relies heavily on Patriot systems to defend against Russian missile attacks, while countries in the Middle East also require the systems to protect against Iranian missile threats.The US therefore has to balance its own stockpile requirements with commitments to allies.The issue goes beyond the Iran conflict. US defence planners are also worried about the possibility of a future conflict with China, particularly over Taiwan.A prolonged conflict in the Middle East has demonstrated how quickly sophisticated weapons can be consumed during sustained combat.If US stocks remain depleted for years, Washington could face a difficult situation in which it has to manage military commitments in the Middle East, Europe and the Indo-Pacific simultaneously.CSIS has described the prolonged rebuilding timelines as creating a potential "window of vulnerability" for the US.The concern is particularly acute for weapons such as long-range precision missiles and advanced air-defence interceptors, which would also be required in a high-intensity conflict in the Western Pacific.Trump disputes reports of weapons shortagesPresident Donald Trump has repeatedly rejected reports that the US is running dangerously low on ammunition.On Thursday, Trump said the US has "massive amounts" of weapons and added that "large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed."Trump has also criticised reports suggesting that he confronted Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over depleted weapons stocks.Responding to a Washington Post report on Truth Social, Trump said he was "extremely happy" with Hegseth's performance and accused the newspaper of spreading "false and completely unfounded rumours"."The Fake News, as usual, is spreading false and completely unfounded rumours. I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing," Trump wrote.The White House and Pentagon have denied claims that Trump confronted Hegseth over weapons shortages at a Camp David meeting.White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said the reported confrontation "literally never happened", while Parnell said Hegseth had not misled Trump about US ammunition supplies.The Pentagon's position is that the US military currently has enough weapons to conduct its operations.Parnell has said the department has everything required for current military operations, while Conley separately said the US has sufficient munitions "for the task at hand".That does not necessarily contradict the concerns about depleted inventories.The distinction is between having enough weapons to fight today and having enough weapons to sustain prolonged combat or prepare for another major war.The Pentagon can maintain that it has sufficient munitions for current operations while simultaneously ordering industry to accelerate production because replacing what has already been fired could take years.The Pentagon's demand could lead to a major expansion of the US defence industrial base.Companies will face pressure to increase production rates, build new facilities and strengthen supply chains.Lockheed Martin, RTX, Northrop Grumman and other major contractors are already investing in expanded production.But the industry faces its own constraints. Production capacity cannot be expanded instantly, particularly for highly specialised missile components.The Pentagon's latest directive therefore represents an attempt to push defence companies to move faster while the government provides the contracts and funding needed to support expansion.Parnell said the initiative would "inform the fiscal year 2028 budget submitted to Congress for funding" and was consistent with the Pentagon's effort to rebuild the defence industrial base.The production push is also taking place against a broader fight over US defence spending.A defence spending bill is currently stalled in Congress as lawmakers debate President Trump's military action against Iran and the administration's request to substantially increase Pentagon spending.The White House has sought a defence budget of about $1.5 trillion, compared with roughly $900 billion the previous year.Any major expansion of missile production will require substantial government funding.But even if Congress approves the money, the physical expansion of production lines and supply chains will still take time.
Article Summary: Pentagon asks defence firms to ramp up weapons production. Comes amid reports that stocks of key air-defence interceptors have fallen sharply from pre-war levels. US officials have rejected suggestions that the military has run out of weapons needed for current operations.

Article Title: Colombia rocked by car bomb blast a day after new President Abelardo de la Espriella takes charge
Article Text:
Car bomb hits Colombia's southwest as new President Abelardo de la Espriella takes charge

A car bomb exploded Saturday at a toll plaza in southwestern Colombia, the army said, a day after conservative political newcomer Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in as the country's new president.The army blamed the attack on two dissident groups of the now-defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), which rejected the peace agreement the guerrilla group signed with the Colombian government a decade ago.The blast took place at a toll plaza on the Pan-American Highway, a key road linking Colombia's southwestern regions. Two security guards suffered minor injuries, according to the army. One of the guards told authorities that the explosion was caused by a vehicle abandoned at the site by a person who fled on a motorcycle.The affected stretch of highway connects the departments of Cauca and Valle del Cauca, whose capital, Cali, hosted de la Espriella's inauguration on Friday. In his inaugural address, the new president laid out his security policy and warned armed groups that “they have two paths: submit to the rule of law or confront the security forces.”On Saturday, the army said soldiers had secured the area and deployed trained dogs to search for any additional explosives.Parts of the vehicle, including its charred chassis, were scattered around the toll plaza.The blast woke families living just metres from the scene. Elizabeth Zapata, 57, said the force of the explosion “lift them out of bed” and shattered the windows of nearby homes. Her family, which includes several children, “arrived with shards of glass embedded in their backs.”Cauca Governor Jorge Octavio Guzmán said he believed the attacks were aimed at isolating the department and allowing armed groups to maintain control over thousands of hectares.“This is not an isolated incident; it is systematic," he said.Transportation Minister Elsa Noguera condemned the attack and said efforts were underway to restore traffic along the affected route.“Colombia will not kneel before violence, nor will it allow the destruction of the infrastructure that connects our regions,” she wrote on social media.Dozens of prisoners transferred to maximum-security prisonsAlso on Saturday, de la Espriella announced the transfer of 117 prisoners linked to peace talks under the previous administration to eight maximum-security prisons.According to the country's corrections agency, the move is intended to “regain permanent control of the prisons” and “contain any capacity of criminal organizations” to coordinate illicit activities from inside prisons.De la Espriella has rejected the dialogue with armed groups pursued by his predecessor, Gustavo Petro.The 48-year-old lawyer and businessman, who had no prior political experience, narrowly defeated progressive senator and Petro ally Iván Cepeda in a June runoff election held against the backdrop of a deeply polarised political climate.His presidency begins with a strong opposition led by Petro, who refused to recognise de la Espriella's victory and alleged electoral fraud despite the official declaration by Colombia's electoral authority and favourable assessments from international observers.
Article Summary: The army blames the attack on two dissident groups of the now-defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia. The blast took place at a toll plaza on the Pan-American Highway, a key road linking Colombia's southwestern regions. The army said soldiers had secured the area and deployed trained dogs to search for any additional explosives.

Article Title: Dozens of Nigerians freed after six months in jihadi captivity
Article Text:
The Nigerians were abducted on Feb 3 when jihadi militants stormed the village of Woro, killing over 160 others.

Some of the 163 kidnapped Nigerians rescued from jihadi captivity have spoken of the suffering and fear they lived in for six months. The freed captives, mostly women and children, were among over 300 kidnap victims freed by Nigerian forces this week. They were handed over to the authorities by security forces in Ilorin, the capital of Kwara state, on Friday for medical attention and routine checks, and were anticipating their return home to reunite with their families.Mary Ishaya recalled days without food, and being asked alongside others to bury other hostages who died in captivity. The 44-year-old, who had never touched a dead body, said: “I still cannot find the right words to describe what has happened to us. We saw death and suffering.”The Nigerians were abducted on Feb 3 when jihadi militants stormed the village of Woro, killing over 160 others. In the hospital where they were receiving medical attention, the freed captives looked emaciated with many laying on the floor, barely able to stand, while others had injuries and emotional scars from their ordeal. Some of the women were informed that their husbands had been among those killed in the Feb attack.Some said they had given up on any hope of returning home. Others recounted people falling sick, being beaten by the rain, and told to hide whenever Nigerian military helicopters flew over the forest hideouts where the captors held them.The US is providing military support to Nigeria under an agreement it says aims to protect Nigerian Christians, though much of that support is restricted to logistics and intelligence-gathering.
Article Summary: The freed captives, mostly women and children, were among over 300 kidnap victims freed by Nigerian forces this week. They were handed over to the authorities by security forces in Ilorin, the capital of Kwara state, on Friday. The Nigerians were abducted on Feb 3 when jihadi militants stormed the village of Woro.

Article Title: Video: 2 injured after gunman opens fire near New York subway station
Article Text:
NYPD said a 20-year-old and a 31-year-old man were injured in the Bronx shooting.

Two men were injured after a gunman opened fire near a busy subway station in New York City's Bronx on Thursday evening, NY police said.The shooting happened at around 6 p.m. outside the West Farms Square-E Tremont Avenue subway station. Surveillance footage from the area showed a man wearing a white hoodie walking towards a plaza before firing several shots in the direction of a group gathered near a shop.Video from the scene also captured people fleeing as the gunman escaped. One man was seen tumbling over a bench and rolling onto the pavement, although it was not immediately clear whether he had been hit by gunfire.According to the New York Police Department (NYPD), a 20-year-old man was shot in the leg, while a 31-year-old man suffered a gunshot wound to the buttocks.Both victims were taken to St. Barnabas Hospital, where they were reported to be in stable condition.Police have not confirmed whether the two injured men were the intended targets or were caught in the gunfire by chance.The suspect fled the scene after the shooting. No arrests had been announced as of Thursday night, and the investigation remains ongoing.
Article Summary: The shooting happened at around 6 p.m. outside the West Farms Square-E Tremont Avenue subway station in New York City's Bronx. A 20-year-old man was shot in the leg, while a 31-year old man suffered a gunshot wound to the buttocks. Both victims were taken to St Barnabas Hospital, where they were reported to be in stable condition.

Article Title: PhD student Vikram Mubayi found dead in lake after going missing on solo hiking trip in US
Article Text:
UC Santa Barbara PhD student Vikram Mubayi was found dead after going missing during a solo hike in California's Inyo National Forest.

Vikram Mubayi, a chemical engineering PhD student at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), was found dead on August 3 in California's Inyo National Forest, two days after he went missing during a solo hiking trip in the Big Pine Lakes area.According to local reports, Mubayi last contacted his family on the evening of August 1 before a search operation was launched by Inyo County Search & Rescue.Authorities later recovered Mubayi's body from Big Pine Lakes, and officials said the circumstances surrounding his death remain under investigation, with no indication of foul play.Born and raised in Hong Kong, Mubayi was described by his family as an experienced hiker.In a post on Reddit, his sibiling urged people to inform if someone had seen Vikram. "My brother Vikram is 6’3, 170lbs, dark hair, and has been out of contact since 8.30pm yesterday in the big pine lakes area in the eastern sierra, specifically around agassiz col. Have attached a link to his route here strava.com/routes/3516945857263630584. Did anyone happen to see him along the way? he last sent an update 8.37PM PST from the following coordinates: 37.10942° N, 118.52428° W" the post said."He’s a fairly experienced hiker and we think that he reached a reasonably easy part of the route, so would have expected him back by now. his car is still at the trailhead. So sorry if this is not the right place to post. can post somewhere else if there’s a better place," it added.The official confirmation is yet to come from the authorities.
Article Summary: Vikram Mubayi, a chemical engineering PhD student at the University of California, Santa Barbara, was found dead on August 3 in California's Inyo National Forest. The circumstances surrounding his death remain under investigation, with no indication of foul play.
