Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian was reportedly taken to a secret location in Tehran and granted only a brief meeting with a man introduced as Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, according to Iran International.The reported encounter, conducted inside a dark, tinted-window vehicle, has fuelled fresh questions over the secrecy surrounding Iran's leadership.According to the report, Pezeshkian was unable to see the man seated beside him and later questioned whether the voice he heard had indeed belonged to the country's new supreme leader.Their account of what they described as the only known meeting between the president and Iran's third supreme leader differs markedly from Pezeshkian's public version of events.Speaking at a gathering of trade association representatives in mid-May, Pezeshkian said he had spent two and a half hours with the new leader in what he described as a "cordial atmosphere."However, the report said that the meeting lasted only a few minutes, after which the president was asked to leave.According to the report, the meeting took place only after Pezeshkian repeatedly sought an audience with the supreme leader and threatened to resign.They said the leader's office agreed to the meeting under pressure but informed the president that, unlike previous practice, he would not be received at the supreme leader's official residence.Instead, Pezeshkian's security team reportedly took him to an undisclosed location in Tehran, where he was escorted from his vehicle into the back seat of a dark, tinted-window commercial car. The report claimed the supreme leader was already inside, but the vehicle was kept dark enough that the two men could not see each other. They also alleged that Khamenei's security personnel did not allow a handshake, and the conversation took place entirely by voice.The reported arrangement left Pezeshkian feeling humiliated, as per the report.Officials in the president's office told Iran International that he later questioned whether the person beside him had actually been the supreme leader, as he had only heard a voice during the brief meeting.Pezeshkian had earlier acknowledged that communicating with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei is "very difficult.""It is very difficult to communicate with him at the moment, but in any case, his presence is a very great source of strength for us so that we can continue," Pezeshkian said.Mojtaba Khamenei has continued to issue written statements, but his absence from public view since assuming Iran's top leadership has fuelled speculation about his relationship with senior officials and his whereabouts. Nearly five months after the Assembly of Experts selected him to succeed his father as supreme leader, no audio recording or video of him has been released.The prolonged silence has also drawn attention in Iran's state-aligned media. On Sunday, the Hamshahri newspaper's website published a video claiming that foreign intelligence agencies could use advanced acoustic analysis of audio recordings, including background noise, electrical grid frequency signatures and vocal characteristics, to identify the leader's location or assess his physical condition.The claims appeared to deepen, rather than dispel, speculation surrounding Khamenei's status.Conflicting assessments have also emerged internationally. Three weeks ago, US President Donald Trump said there was a "90 percent" chance that Mojtaba Khamenei had been killed, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has more recently said the Iranian leader is alive.
Article Summary: Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian was reportedly taken to a secret location in Tehran and granted only a brief meeting with a man introduced as Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The reported encounter, conducted inside a dark, tinted-window vehicle, has fuelled fresh questions over the secrecy surrounding Iran's leadership.

Article Title: Watch: Scared Thailand school students duck under desks as gunshots ring out; 8 dead
Article Text:
Video shows Thailand students hiding under desks during school shooting (Image: X@/CatchUpFeed)

At least eight people were killed on Friday after a student opened fire at a school in Thailand before turning the gun on himself, a national police official said.The gunman first shot and killed his grandparents at their home before opening fire at the school.The student fired 26 rounds, while another 34 rounds of ammunition were recovered from the scene, according to a police statement.Videos from the scene showed students ducking under their desks as gunshots could be heard in the background.The shooting took place at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province, northwest of Bangkok. Police identified the shooter as a student.Lt Col Dechrapee Kongdee, commander of the Nonthaburi Provincial Police, confirmed the casualties to Reuters and said the suspected gunman had died by suicide.He said those injured included one teacher and three students.An 18-year-old student said he initially mistook the sound of gunfire for firecrackers going off or someone banging an object."I didn't think ⁠it was a gun at first," he was quoted as saying by Reuters. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again."According to district authorities, the school had around 3,100 students and 147 teachers enrolled during the 2025 academic year.The latest incident comes months after a teacher was killed and a student injured in a separate shooting at a school in Hat Yai district in southern Thailand in February.
Article Summary: Shooting took place at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Bang Kruai district, northwest of Bangkok. Gunman first shot and killed his grandparents at their home before opening fire at the school. Video shows students ducking under their desks as gunshots can be heard in background.

Article Title: Exiled Bangladeshi cricket star Shakib Al Hasan willing to return, face murder trial if safety assured
Article Text:
Bangladesh cricket star Shakib Al Hasan, an exiled ally of ousted PM Sheikh Hasina, says he is ready to return home and face trial on murder charges if the government guarantees his security.

Bangladesh cricket Shakib Al Hasan has said he is willing to return home and face criminal proceedings against him if the government guarantees his safety, according to an exclusive interview with Reuters.Shakib has been living in exile in the United States since former prime minister Sheikh Hasina was ousted in a student-led uprising in August 2024. The former Bangladesh captain, who was also an Awami League lawmaker under Hasina, has not returned home since.“If I get the clearance from the government that my security will be ensured, I am happy to go back, face the court trial and everything that's needed to be done,” Shakib told Reuters by phone from Sri Lanka.He said he believed the allegations against him were baseless and wanted the opportunity to return and defend himself in court. Shakib said he was also keen to speak with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman about his return.Shakib is facing two active cases in Bangladesh. One concerns the alleged killing of a protester during the 2024 uprising, while another was filed by anti-corruption authorities. He said the murder case was filed on a day when he was playing a match in Toronto.Shakib also said his bank accounts had been frozen for around 18 months while investigations continued. He has not appointed a defence lawyer in the murder case, according to Reuters.His political links remain a major obstacle to his return. Shakib defended his decision to appear virtually at a press conference with Hasina in Delhi this week, saying he had only called for peace and progress in Bangladesh. He said he had no intention of distancing himself from Hasina or the Awami League to facilitate his return.The Rahman government, however, has rejected any suggestion of special treatment. His press secretary A.A.M. Saleh told Reuters that Shakib was facing the consequences of his association with the former government and that Bangladeshi law applied equally to everyone.“Shakib Al Hasan is an accused person, and he must surrender before the courts of Bangladesh to face the judicial process,” Saleh said.Shakib said he had previously tried to return. In late 2024, he boarded a flight home after receiving assurances that he would be protected, but was reportedly instructed to turn around while the plane was in transit. He returned to New York after landing in Dubai.A subsequent attempt also failed after he posted a birthday message for Hasina, which authorities cited as a reason for preventing his entry, he said.Despite the political and legal uncertainty, Shakib has not retired from international cricket. He said he wants to play a farewell series at home and hopes to represent Bangladesh at the 2027 ODI World Cup, although he acknowledged that he cannot continue indefinitely.“I am feeling good, still enjoying the game, playing well also,” Shakib told Reuters. “But ... age is not on my side at this moment, so I cannot wait for too long.”The cricketer also said he has not seen his parents in Bangladesh for two years and that the prolonged separation had been difficult for his family.
Article Summary: Bangladesh cricket star Shakib Al Hasan says he is willing to return home and face criminal proceedings against him if the government guarantees his safety. Shakib has been living in exile in the United States since former prime minister Sheikh Hasina was ousted in a student-led uprising in August 2024. The former Bangladesh captain, who was also an Awami League lawmaker under Hasina, has not returned home since.

Article Title: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan & Turkey sign 'Mecca' pact for mutual defence; India reacts
Article Text:
Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan each bring distinct strategic strengths to the partnership.

Deal amid turbulent West Asia

3 distinct strategic strengths

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey Friday signed a trilateral defence agreement aimed at strengthening their collective security as the conflict involving Iran continues to fuel instability across the West Asia.The agreement was signed following a joint defence summit attended by Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani prime minister Shehbaz Sharif, who attended after performing the Umrah pilgrimage in the city.According to Pakistan's foreign ministry, the pact is "guided by the longstanding historical ties among the three states, based on the enduring bonds of brotherhood and Islamic solidarity that unite them, and building upon their shared strategic interests and longstanding defence cooperation".The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all, they said in a joint statement.The Pakistani ministry said the agreement reflects "the three states’ shared commitment to further strengthening their collective security and to promoting peace, security, and stability in the region and beyond, in pursuit of a secure and prosperous future."Also read: Evening news wrap: CBI chargesheet alleges NTA's own experts leaked NEET-UG, MEA rejects US criticism of of FCRA Bill & more It added that "The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression, and stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all."Meanwhile, India reacted to the development, saying "developments were closely watched".Responding to reports on the agreement, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said: “The pact between the three countries is, again, a development that we are closely following, and we will keep you updated on that.”The deal comes as Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries continue to face missile attacks and disruptions to energy shipments amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran and its regional allies. The war escalated after the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran on February 28, triggering a wider regional crisis.A Turkish official said the agreement was purely defensive, was not aimed at any particular country and remained open to participation by other regional nations. The official also said it would not replace any existing bilateral or multilateral security arrangements.Analysts said the summit carried significant geopolitical weight at a time of growing uncertainty in the region."The political symbolism of the summit is significant. Three of the Muslim world's most influential states are convening at a moment of heightened uncertainty, demonstrating a growing willingness among regional and middle powers to coordinate more closely on security matters," Abdulaziz Sager, chairman of the Saudi-based Gulf Research Center, told new agency Reuters."If institutionalised and translated into concrete cooperation, the trilateral framework could strengthen the three countries' collective diplomatic and defense weight while contributing to the emergence of a more regionally driven security architecture," Sager added.Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan each bring distinct strategic strengths to the partnership. Turkey has Nato's second-largest military, Saudi Arabia is one of the world's biggest oil exporters and custodian of Islam's holiest sites, while Pakistan is the only Muslim-majority country with nuclear weapons.The agreement follows months of discussions on expanding regional security cooperation. Earlier this year, Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan had said Ankara supported a broader regional security platform to promote stability.Experts believe the pact builds on long-standing military ties among the three countries. Pakistan has trained Saudi security forces for decades, while Turkey and Pakistan have cooperated on defence equipment and military training. Saudi Arabia also signed a major deal in 2023 to purchase Turkish drones.Mansoor Ahmed of the Australian National University's Strategic and Defence Studies Centre said Pakistan and Turkey could contribute advanced defence manufacturing capabilities, while Saudi Arabia could provide financial and technological investment.He added, however, that the new agreement was unlikely to include a nuclear component because Pakistan's nuclear deterrent remains focused on India.Pakistan has also expanded its military presence in Saudi Arabia in recent months by deploying thousands of troops, fighter aircraft, drones and air defence systems. It has simultaneously pursued broader security partnerships with Gulf countries, including talks with Kuwait on an expanded defence arrangement linked to energy cooperation and investment.
Article Summary: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey signed a trilateral defence agreement. The agreement is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression. An armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all. The deal comes as Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries continue to face missile attacks.

Article Title: Strait of Hormuz standoff: What conditions have US, Iran set to reopen waterway
Article Text:
Iran says Hormuz will reopen only after US accepts its demands, while Washington seeks unrestricted commercial shipping. (Donald Trump, Iran President Masoud Pezeshkian)

What Iran wants before reopening the strait

1. An end to US threats against Iran

2. An end to US military action

3. Withdrawal of US naval and air forces involved in the blockade

4. Compensation for damage caused during the conflict

5. Lifting of sanctions

6. Unfreezing Iranian assets

7. No US interference in regional negotiations

What Iran and Oman are negotiating

What the US wants

Washington also wants unrestricted commercial shipping

The US wants Iran to fulfil its commitments

Why the Iran-Oman deal is not enough

What could unlock the Strait of Hormuz

Pezeshkian signals room for negotiations

Iran has made clear that a deal with Oman on a new shipping arrangement for the Strait of Hormuz will not, by itself, reopen the strategic waterway. Tehran says the strait will reopen only after the United States accepts a broader set of Iranian conditions, while Washington has indicated that it is prepared to lift its blockade of Iranian ports once commercial shipping resumes without impediments.The competing positions have emerged as Iran and Oman move closer to an agreement on a new shipping protocol for the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow but critical maritime route through which a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments passed before the conflict.Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran and Muscat were "very close" to an agreement on a new arrangement for shipping through the strait. However, he made clear that the agreement with Oman would not be sufficient on its own to reopen the waterway.The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has also rejected suggestions that the reopening of the strait is simply a matter for the Iran-Oman negotiations.IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi said the reopening of the waterway was "contingent upon the United States accepting Iran's conditions and has no connection to the Iran-Oman negotiations."He later said, "Whenever the United States accepts Iran’s conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will certainly be reopened," according to Iran's Tasnim news agency.The statements point to a much broader dispute than the technical question of how ships will navigate the strait. At the centre of the disagreement are US military operations, sanctions, Iranian assets, compensation for wartime damage and control over shipping through one of the world's most important energy corridors.Iran's demands extend beyond an agreement with Oman on shipping arrangements. According to Al Jazeera, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, has outlined several conditions for reopening the waterway.Tehran wants Washington to stop threatening Iran and end what it sees as continued US pressure against the country.For Iran, reopening the strait is therefore linked to the broader security situation. Tehran has argued that maritime arrangements cannot be separated from the military conflict and the wider confrontation with Washington.Iran wants the United States to halt military action against Iran and its regional allies.The demand comes after months of conflict involving US and Israeli attacks on Iran and Iranian retaliation against US interests and bases in the region.Tehran's position is that a return to normal commercial shipping must be accompanied by a wider reduction in military confrontation.Iran has also demanded the withdrawal of US naval and air forces involved in the blockade.The presence of US forces around the waterway has become a central point of contention. Washington has said it controls the blockade and has linked any lifting of restrictions to Iran meeting its commitments.US President Donald Trump said the US Navy was leading the blockade and that Washington controlled it."I don't want to say it has been... it's sort of open right now. We have a thing called the blockade headed up by the US Navy, and we control it. But they can always shoot something or drop a mine... if you have one mine sitting out there, you sort of mess things up because people don't want to take their billion-dollar boats and accidentally get hit by a mine. But I think we're doing very well. I am involved in the negotiations. I think we are doing fine... it could be soon."Another major Iranian demand is compensation from the US for damage caused during the conflict.Iran has indicated that an agreement on shipping cannot be separated from the economic and physical damage it says has resulted from the US military campaign.Araghchi has specifically said that US compensation to Iran would have to be addressed before the strait could reopen.Iran also wants US sanctions imposed on the country to be lifted.Sanctions have been one of the principal tools used by Washington to pressure Tehran. For Iran, their removal would represent a broader economic component of any agreement to end the confrontation.Tehran has also demanded that Iranian assets frozen under US sanctions be released.This would give Iran access to funds that have been restricted as part of the sanctions regime and would form another major element of the economic settlement Tehran is seeking.The IRGC has separately insisted that Washington must stop interfering in regional negotiations.Mohebbi said reopening the strait depended on "specific mechanisms and conditions" and was separate from the negotiations between Iran and Oman.This is important because Oman has been playing a role in discussions over the shipping arrangement. Iran appears to be treating the Oman talks as a mechanism for resolving the technical and legal aspects of maritime traffic, while insisting that the United States must separately meet its political and military conditions.Iran and Oman are working on a new arrangement governing shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Araghchi said the previous shipping traffic separation scheme was no longer acceptable to Tehran. Iran is therefore discussing a temporary route with Oman while technical and legal questions surrounding a permanent route are resolved.The proposed arrangement is aimed at allowing commercial shipping to resume while addressing Iran's concerns over how vessels enter and leave the Persian Gulf.According to Reuters, a proposed deal could give Iran control over ships entering the Gulf through the strait. A senior Iranian source and two regional officials were cited as saying this would represent a major concession to Tehran.However, US officials have repeatedly indicated that Washington would not accept Iran controlling access to the world's most important energy trade route.This disagreement over who controls shipping is therefore one of the most difficult elements of the proposed arrangement.Washington's position is different from Tehran's.The US has indicated that it wants commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz to resume without impediments and has tied the lifting of its blockade to Iran fulfilling its commitments.A US official told Reuters, "There is progress between Oman and Iran on the strait, and we expect a deal soon. Once the deal is announced to restore commercial shipping without impediments, the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports."The official added, "As always, US actions will continue to be performance-based and tied to Iran’s implementation of its commitments."This suggests that Washington sees the reopening of the strait as part of a reciprocal process. Iran would have to meet its commitments before the US takes corresponding steps.The US position centres on restoring normal commercial traffic through the waterway.Washington does not appear willing to accept an arrangement under which Iran has unrestricted authority to decide which ships can enter or leave the Persian Gulf.The issue is particularly important because the strait is a global energy chokepoint. Disruption there affects oil and gas shipments far beyond Iran and the Gulf region.Washington has also made clear that any concessions would be conditional.The US official said American actions would remain "performance-based", meaning Washington would expect Iran to implement agreed measures before the US follows through on its own commitments.Trump has also linked the broader negotiations to the US objective of preventing Iran from possessing a nuclear weapon.The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and the wider Arabian Sea. Its strategic importance comes from the enormous volume of energy that passes through the narrow waterway.Before the conflict, the strait carried around a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments.That makes any prolonged disruption a global economic issue rather than simply a dispute between Iran and the US.When shipping is threatened, tanker operators face higher insurance costs, longer routes and the risk of vessels being attacked or detained. Energy prices can rise as traders anticipate shortages, adding to inflationary pressure.Iran's actions around the waterway have therefore attracted intense international attention.The UAE said on Saturday that Iran had attacked a carrier affiliated with its state oil company with a missile while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz. No injuries were reported. Iranian authorities did not immediately comment on the allegation.Abu Dhabi National Oil Company has also said that 15 of its vessels had been struck while transiting the strait since the beginning of the conflict, resulting in one crew member being killed and 20 injured.The central problem is that Iran and the US appear to be negotiating different parts of the same crisis.Iran's position: A shipping agreement with Oman can resolve navigation and maritime arrangements, but the Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until Washington accepts Tehran's wider political, military and economic conditions.US position: Washington expects Iran and Oman to reach an arrangement allowing normal commercial shipping, after which the US would lift its blockade of Iranian ports, subject to Iran fulfilling its commitments.This creates a major gap between the two sides. For Iran, reopening the strait is part of a broader settlement with the United States.For Washington, reopening the waterway is more closely tied to Iran's implementation of commitments and the restoration of unrestricted commercial shipping.A deal would likely require progress on several issues at the same time.First, Iran and Oman would need to settle the technical and legal framework governing shipping. Tehran has said the previous traffic separation system is no longer acceptable and wants a temporary arrangement while a permanent system is negotiated.Second, Iran and the US would need to resolve the question of military activity around the waterway. Tehran wants US forces involved in the blockade withdrawn, while Washington wants assurances that commercial vessels can move safely without interference.Third, the two sides would have to address the economic issues raised by Iran, including compensation, sanctions and frozen Iranian assets.Finally, there would need to be agreement on who has authority over vessels using the strait. This could prove especially difficult if Washington opposes any arrangement that gives Tehran effective control over access to the waterway.Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has indicated that Tehran sees an opportunity for diplomacy, even while maintaining that Iran will not surrender what it considers its rights.In a post on X, he said: "The best time to reach an agreement is the current situation. On the path to peace, we will not compromise on the rights of the Iranian nation. The government's main reliance is on domestic capacities and the people. The necessity of a compassionate approach toward the people | People are in two categories; either they are your religious brothers, or they are equal to you in creation."Pezeshkian's comments suggest that Iran remains open to negotiations, but Tehran sees the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz as part of a wider agreement with the US.For Iran, reopening the strait depends on an end to US military action and threats, withdrawal of US forces involved in the blockade, compensation for wartime damage, lifting of sanctions, unfreezing of Iranian assets and an end to US interference in regional talks.The US, meanwhile, wants commercial shipping to resume without restrictions and expects Iran to fulfil its commitments before Washington takes further steps. It also opposes giving Iran unilateral control over the waterway.Oman is trying to help the two sides reach an agreement on shipping through the strait. However, Iran has made clear that an Iran-Oman deal alone will not be enough to reopen the waterway.
Article Summary: Iran says Hormuz will reopen only after US accepts its demands, while Washington seeks unrestricted commercial shipping. Iran and Oman move closer to an agreement on a new shipping protocol for the strait. Iran wants Washington to stop threatening Iran and end what it sees as continued US pressure against the country.

Article Title: Trump forces US oil billionaire to exit Venezuela
Article Text:
The treasury department on Friday froze the assets of Sargeant’s offshore company that participates in Venezuelan oil-producing ventures, according to sources

The Trump administration is dialling up pressure on Florida oil magnate and Republican Party donor Harry Sargeant III to divest from Venezuela. The treasury department on Friday froze the assets of Sargeant's offshore company that participates in Venezuelan oil-producing ventures, according to sources. It also issued a license that would allow him to unwind his interests in the firm, the people said. Sargeant served as a vital back channel between Washington and Caracas during years of deep hostility, accumulating outsized influence on both sides. The department can use a variety of measures to block financial transactions with entities that run afoul of US foreign policy.
Article Summary: The treasury department on Friday froze the assets of Sargeant’s offshore company that participates in Venezuelan oil-producing ventures, according to sources. It also issued a license that would allow him to unwind his interests in the firm, the people said. The department can use a variety of measures to block financial transactions with entities that run afoul of US foreign policy.

Article Title: US rejects China’s Scarborough Reef measures, backs Philippines in South China Sea dispute
Article Text:
The United States alleged that China was using environmental and legal justifications to advance broader maritime claims across the South China Sea.

The United States has rejected China’s attempts to enforce what it called a destabilising “national nature reserve” at Scarborough Reef. It said that Beijing is using environmental and legal measures to strengthen its territorial claims in the South China Sea while restricting Filipino fishermen’s access to traditional fishing grounds.In a statement issued on 8 August, US state department spokesperson Thomas “Tommy” Pigott said Washington opposes China’s ongoing efforts at Scarborough Reef and reaffirmed US support for the Philippines, a treaty ally, in promoting a free and open Indo-Pacific.The statement accused Beijing of attempting to deny Filipino fishermen access to waters recognised under the 2016 Arbitral Award and described China’s actions as coercive and unilateral.“The United States rejects China’s ongoing attempts to enforce its destabilizing ‘national nature reserve’ at Scarborough Reef and deny Filipino fishermen access to their traditional fishing ground as reflected in the 2016 Arbitral Award,” Pigott said.The United States further alleged that China was using environmental and legal justifications to advance broader maritime claims across the South China Sea.“This is yet another unilateral attempt by China to use dubious environmental and legal pretexts, backed by coercion, to advance its sweeping territorial and maritime claims in the South China Sea at the expense of its neighbours,” the statement said.Washington also reiterated its commitment to the Philippines amid continuing tensions in the disputed waters.“The United States stands with our Ally, the Philippines, in support of a free and open Indo-Pacific,” Pigott said.Scarborough Reef has remained one of the most contested areas in the South China Sea, where China, the Philippines and several other countries have overlapping territorial and maritime claims. The 2016 international arbitration ruling found that China’s expansive claims had no legal basis under international law, although Beijing has rejected the ruling and continued to assert control over areas within the disputed sea.
Article Summary: The United States has rejected China’s attempts to enforce what it called a destabilising ‘national nature reserve’ at Scarborough Reef. It said that Beijing is using environmental and legal measures to strengthen its territorial claims in the South China Sea. Washington also reiterated its commitment to the Philippines amid continuing tensions.

Article Title: Kash Patel plans Russia trip in October; Kremlin-friendly newspaper warns he better not come empty-handed if he has a favor to ask
Article Text:
FBI Director Kash Patel is scheduled to visit Russia in mid-October.

What we know about Kash Patel's planned Russia visit

FBI director Kash Patel is planning to visit Russia in mid-October at a time when Washington and Moscow continue to be at odds over the war in Ukraine, Politico reported, calling any such planned visit from the FBi chief as "unusual and sensitive". Patel has a history of involvement in controversial Russia-related matters dating to President Donald Trump’s first term, including trying to cast doubt on investigations into whether Trump colluded with Russia to help him win the 2016 election and Patel also is developing a track record of taking eye-catching trips in his role atop the FBI, drawing scrutiny from Congress, the report said.Reacting to the news, a Kremlin-friendly newspaper Moskovsky Komsomolets said the FBi director better not come empty-handed if he is coming to ask a favor. “It’s assumed that Russia has some kind of dirt on the Democrats, and we could provide it, in one form or another, to the American side,” Vladimir Vasiliev of the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Arbatov Institute for U.S. and Canadian Studies told the newspaper, speculating on the possible reasons for Patel’s visit.Vasiliev works closely with the Russian International Affairs Council, overseen by President Vladimir Putin’s top diplomat, Sergei Lavrov, as the chairman of the board.“At the same time, the Americans might also have something to share, seeing as the Russian side could ask, ‘What do we get in return? or inquire, ‘What do you have to say about this or that issue?’” he asked.Politico cited US officials familiar with Patel's travel plans and confirmed that Patel is scheduled to visit Russia on Oct. 14-15, first stopping in Moscow and then St Petersburg.Patel's host is likely to be the FSB, the Russian security service that is heir to the Soviet-era KGB.It’s not clear if Patel will meet with Russian leader Vladimir Putin or any of his senior political aides. Also unclear is what is on his agenda for discussion.Robert Mueller was the last FBI director known to have visited Russia, in 2013. Mueller was later appointed as a special counsel to investigate ties between the 2016 Trump presidential campaign and Russia, as well as broader Russian efforts to interfere in US elections.
Article Summary: FBI director Kash Patel is planning to visit Russia in mid-October. The visit comes at a time when Washington and Moscow continue to be at odds over the war in Ukraine. It's not clear if Patel will meet with Russian leader Vladimir Putin or any of his senior political aides.

Article Title: Quote of the day on love: 'Find what you love and let it kill you'
Article Text:
Quote of the day on love, its meaning and origin.

The meaning of the quote

Who was Kinky Friedman?

The famous line "find what you love and let it kill you" is almost universally attributed to Charles Bukowski, though history tells a slightly more complicated story. Literature scholars and researchers have found no evidence that Bukowski ever wrote or spoke those exact words in his books, poems, or letters. The phrase actually originated with the Texas musician and author Kinky Friedman in the 1980s. Yet, despite being a misattribution, millions of people attach the quote to Bukowski.The earliest documented appearance of the phrase came from an interview in April 1998, when musician Van Dyke Parks quoted his longtime friend: "It's like my friend Kinky Friedman said: 'You've got to find what you love and let it kill you. I don't think any of us should ever forget that.'" When asked about the origin of the line, Friedman confirmed that it was a pure "Kinky-ism" of his own creation.At its core, the quote presents a bold idea: since time eventually wears down every human life, individuals should consciously choose the passion or obsession that consumes their limited years.Human existence is inherently temporary. Everyone gives away energy, hours, and health to something over time.Many people drift through life allowing dull routines, meaningless stress, or unwanted obligations to drain their vitality without receiving anything fulfilling in return. This quote urges a rejection of that passive decay. Instead of letting life wear you away by accident, it encourages you to pour your spirit into a cause, craft, or passion that truly matters to you.To let something kill you, in this figurative sense, does not mean seeking physical harm. It means surrendering comfort, safety, and self-doubt to serve a singular purpose. It describes a devotion so intense that it absorbs your daily focus, shapes your choices, and defines your legacy. Whether that pursuit is creative work, deep relationships, scientific discovery, or a lifelong belief, the statement suggests that giving everything to a meaningful obsession gives direction to an otherwise random existence.The phrase also acts as a warning against safe indifference. Living a cautious life where you never risk failure or heartbreak might protect you from disappointment, but it also deprives you of deep passion. The quote argues that a life spent burning brightly for something you genuinely care about is far superior to a quiet, prolonged life spent in total detachment.Ultimately, this idea challenges everyone to audit their priorities and ask a fundamental question: what is worthy of your time and energy? It pushes people to find a purpose strong enough to justify sacrifice. When you devote yourself entirely to something you love, you transform the passage of time from a slow march toward the end into a deliberate, deeply fulfilling journey.Richard Samet "Kinky" Friedman (1944–2024) was a uniquely American figure: a country singer, satirist, mystery novelist, and independent politician. Known for his trademark Stetson hat, unlit cigar, denim jackets, and sharp, dark wit, Friedman built a career around refusing to fit neatly into any conventional box.
Article Summary: The famous line "find what you love and let it kill you" is almost universally attributed to Charles Bukowski. The phrase actually originated with Texas musician and author Kinky Friedman in the 1980s. At its core, the quote presents a bold idea: since time eventually wears down every human life, individuals should consciously choose the passion or obsession that consumes their limited years.

Article Title: ‘He did not make it’: Death of PhD student Vikram Mubayi after California hike leaves family seeking answers
Article Text:
Vikram Mubayi.

Who was Vikram Mubayi?

Researcher and avid outdoorsman

Vikram Mubayi, a chemical engineering PhD student at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), died after going missing during a solo hike in California’s Eastern Sierra, with his family now left seeking answers over what happened.Mubayi’s brother, who had earlier appealed for help on Reddit, later shared an update confirming that search-and-rescue teams had found his brother deceased.“Unfortunately SAR confirmed that my brother did not make it,” he wrote, thanking everyone who had offered kind words and support during the search. He also thanked those who were “so generous” as to go out and join the search.The brother said he might not respond to further messages but wanted those who had helped to know that he appreciated their support and wished he could respond to everyone individually.Mubayi was reported missing after his family lost contact with him during a weekend trip to the Big Pine Lakes area of Inyo National Forest.His last contact with his family was around 8:37 pm on August 1, when he was hiking near Agassiz Col. Mubayi’s vehicle was still at the trailhead when he went missing. He was carrying a Garmin satellite device and had shared his GPS coordinates with his family.Inyo County Search and Rescue personnel and the California Highway Patrol joined the search.Mubayi’s remains were recovered from the Big Pine Lakes area on August 3.Authorities have not released a cause or manner of death. Investigators said there is currently no evidence of foul play and that the circumstances remain under investigation.Born and raised in Hong Kong, Mubayi earned a bachelor’s degree in chemical engineering from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign in 2022. He worked there as a research assistant and teaching assistant before pursuing his PhD at UCSB.At UCSB, Mubayi worked in the O’Malley Lab, where his research focused on anaerobic bacteria that can break down lignin, a tough component of plant matter.His work explored biological approaches to converting plant waste and plastics into more sustainable alternatives to petroleum-based materials.Mubayi was also passionate about hiking, tennis and cycling. In 2022, he took part in Illini 4000, a student-led nonprofit initiative, cycling from New York to San Francisco to raise money for cancer research and patient support services.His family had described him as a fairly experienced hiker in their earlier appeal for help. A university profile also noted his interest in applying chemical and biological engineering to environmental sustainability and climate change.
Article Summary: Vikram Mubayi, a chemical engineering PhD student at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), died after going missing during a solo hike in California’s Eastern Sierra. His brother, who had earlier appealed for help on Reddit, later shared an update confirming that search-and-rescue teams had found his brother deceased.

Article Title: ICE arrests at airports: Immigration lawyers share these 6 tips if you are stopped, questioned or detained

ICE increased its presence at domestic airports leading to a sharp uptick in the number of daily arrests.

Do not sign anything: 6 things to do

American Immigration Lawyers' Association issued a travel alert for visa holders.

Stay calm: If stopped by ICE agents at an airport, there is no use of running, arguing or physically resisting. One must stay calm. Present your passport if asked: You may show your passport as ID. You are not required to disclose your visa category. Opt out of facial scan: The association urged individuals to say, "I am opting out of facial recognition. I want manual ID verification". Remain silent: Say, "I am exercising my right to remain silent". Ask for a lawyer: Say, "I want to speak to an attorney". Repeat if necessary. Do not sign anything: Before signing on any immigration form, speak with your attorney.

Who are at higher risk?

Documents to carry

Passport

I-94 printout

I-797 approval

ICE has a goal of 2000 immigration arrests per day

As ICE arrests at domestic airports have seen a sharp uptick in recent weeks, the American Immigration Lawyers Association shared six tips for visa holders to do once they are stopped, questioned, or detained. Many people do not check the date.Those who have certain criminal cases such as DUI or drug chargeThe immigration lawyers association identified certain states as high-risk like Alabama, Texas and Florida as they have laws that create added rosk and may result in immigration detention or arrest during a routine traffic stop.Reports claimed that the department has given ICE a target of daily 2,000 immigration arrests, for which the recent drive has begun. Article Title: Major US university to hide letter grades for first-semester students, cites ‘mental health crisis’
Article Text:
University of Michigan. (AP Photo)

‘Curb the mental health crisis’

Freshmen automatically included

Other US colleges have similar system

A major US university is set to stop showing letter grades for first-semester freshmen in an effort to help students adjust to college life and address what it calls a growing mental health crisis among college-aged students.The University of Michigan’s College of Literature, Science and the Arts (LSA) will introduce the first-semester grade-covering programme from fall 2027, according to the college.Students will continue receiving their actual grades and feedback from professors, but their first-semester results will appear on transcripts only as “pass” or “no credit”, the New York Post reported.The grades will not be included in students’ GPAs during their first semester. However, the university will maintain the actual grades internally for purposes including academic awards, scholarships, internships, financial aid, athletic eligibility and academic advising.The university said the initiative is designed to help freshmen “establish early momentum” and acclimatise to the demands of college without the pressure of grades affecting their academic records.“We believe that covering grades will help students start strong and curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals,” the college said.LSA said the programme would also encourage students to explore unfamiliar subjects without worrying that a poor first-semester grade could have long-term consequences.All first-year LSA students will be covered under the programme, rather than being allowed to opt in. The college said making it optional could undermine the programme by making students feel that covered grades indicate poor performance.Students will begin receiving conventional letter grades that count towards their GPAs from their second semester. New transfer students will not be eligible for the programme.Michigan is not the first US university to adopt a similar approach. The Massachusetts Institute of Technology has used a pass/no-record grading system for first-year students during the fall semester since 1968, with conventional letter grades beginning in the spring.The University of Michigan’s LSA is its largest college, with nearly 20,000 undergraduates, including more than 3,500 first-year students as of fall 2025.
Article Summary: The University of Michigan will introduce the first-semester grade-covering programme from fall 2027. Grades will not be included in students’ GPAs during their first semester. The university will maintain the actual grades internally for purposes including academic awards, scholarships, internships and financial aid.

Article Title: Donald Trump shoots from Senate shoulders to punish Russia, by making India and China pay
Article Text:
File photo: US President Donald Trump

TOI correspondant from Washington:

The US Senate on Friday approved a bill that will allow President Trump to impose 100% tariffs on the world's top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas, including India, China, and Turkey.The legislation also targets countries helping Russia evade energy sanctions, Russian banks, officials, and so-called oligarchs and shadow fleet of tankers.By an overwhelming 86-11 vote, senators approved the Graham bill, formally the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, a sweeping legislation named for the late Republican Senator, war hawk, and staunch Ukraine supporter, who died July 11. The bill now heads to the House, so the US President does not yet have a new 100% tariff bazooka just yet.Trump’s tariff menu has now become rather like a Washington restaurant: reciprocal tariffs, national-security tariffs, sectoral tariffs, country tariffs, Russia tariffs, China tariffs, and today's chef's special, “100% punitive tariff, subject to presidential discretion.” Tariff hee tariff, as they would say in India.There is an important difference, however. Most of Trump's earlier tariffs were justified as instruments to correct trade deficits, protect American industry or respond to “unfair trade practices.”This one is explicitly a secondary sanction: India or China could be punished not for what they sell America, but for whom they buy energy from, a considerably more muscular and explosive use of American market power.India gets a particularly awkward deja vu, having already been through this news reel just months ago and seemingly coming out of it. In August 2025, Trump imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian goods because India was buying Russian oil, taking the combined tariff on many Indian imports to 50%. Washington subsequently removed that additional 25% in February 2026 after India agreed to stop buying Russian oil as part of a broader trade deal (which now appears to be in coma). The US then reduced its reciprocal tariff on India to 18%.The new bill therefore raises an obvious question: if India has already been rewarded for abandoning Russian oil, why give the president another legal switch with which to threaten it? Because geopolitics, apparently, now comes with an erratic reset button wielded by a mercurial President.A 100% tariff would not necessarily mean all that trade disappears, the bill gives Trump discretion, and there are national-interest waiver provisions and exemptions. Allies and partners can also qualify for exemptions by taking meaningful steps to reduce dependence on Russian energy.India, meanwhile, has an unusually strong reason to resist: energy security. Russian oil has become an important component of its crude supply, and Indian refiners have been buying Russian crude in large quantities, particularly after disruptions to Middle Eastern supply. In March-May alone, India settled roughly $14.6 billion of imports in rupees, a surge largely associated with Russian oil purchases.The Trump administration's tariff record makes the new measure particularly intriguing. Tariffs have been threatened, announced, postponed, imposed, doubled, negotiated down, exempted, replaced and, after the Supreme Court intervened, revoked, only for alternative tariffs to appear through different statutory authorities.The administration's original broad IEEPA tariffs were terminated after the Supreme Court ruled in February that the president could not use that emergency-powers law to impose them. Yet tariffs did not exactly die; they merely changed legal wardrobes.The distinction matters because the Graham bill would give Congress itself a statutory framework for imposing punitive tariffs on major Russian-energy customers; it is therefore less of an executive improvisation and more of a congressional authorization for economic coercion.But most analysts assert tariff eventually is not a cheque from Beijing or New Delhi made payable to Uncle Sam; American importers would face the tariff first, with much of the cost likely passed along to American consumers or absorbed partly by suppliers and companies.The Federal Reserve found that tariffs imposed through November 2025 had raised core-goods prices by 3.1% through February 2026, accounting for essentially all the excess inflation in that category. The Yale Budget Lab estimates current tariffs will ultimately raise the US consumer price level by about 0.7%, costing the average household roughly $1,100 a year.So while President Trump claims the US is collecting billions in tariff revenue, Americans also pay billions more for imported goods and inputs.The tariff is therefore rather less like discovering oil under the White House lawn and rather more like charging yourself admission to your own amusement park.If the policy drives buyers into alternative suppliers, raises global oil prices, encourages more trade outside the dollar system or triggers retaliation against American exports, the tariff cannon can develop the traditional artillery problem: the recoil is felt by the person firing it.
Article Summary: The US Senate on Friday approved a bill that will allow President Trump to impose 100% tariffs on the world's top five purchasers of Russian oil or natural gas. The bill now heads to the House, so the US President does not yet have a new 100% tariff bazooka just yet.

Article Title: Utah girl Emma Meline was diagnosed with severe aplastic anemia days before Christmas; her 2-year-old sister became her perfect bone marrow match
Article Text:
Emma Meline (Image Credit: GoFundMe)

A sudden diagnosis

The Meline sisters (Image Credit: Amanda Meline via PEOPLE)

Family searched for match

Sister becomes donor

A long road to recovery

A life-changing bond

(Source: GoFundMe, PEOPLE’s exclusive report)

A Utah family’s difficult medical journey took an emotional turn when young Emma Meline was diagnosed with severe aplastic anemia just days before Christmas, and about two months later, the family learned that her 2-year-old sister was a perfect bone marrow match. According to a GoFundMe fundraiser organised by Emma’s mother, Amanda Meline, Emma began experiencing concerning symptoms on December 21, 2025, and was soon diagnosed with bone marrow failure and severe aplastic anemia. The family later learned that Emma’s younger sister, Lucy, could donate the marrow needed for her transplant.Emma’s health concerns began shortly before Christmas 2025. Her parents noticed symptoms that worried them, prompting a visit to her pediatrician. She was then sent for further testing and biopsies, which led to a diagnosis of bone marrow failure and severe aplastic anemia.The condition affects the bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones responsible for producing blood cells. In people with aplastic anemia, the marrow does not make enough new red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. As a result, patients can become vulnerable to infections, fatigue, bleeding and other serious complications.According to the family's GoFundMe page, Emma required repeated care at Primary Children’s Hospital in Salt Lake City and was treated on an immunocompromised services unit. Her family described her condition as extremely rare and said even relatively minor illnesses could become serious because of her weakened immune system.Following Emma’s diagnosis, her parents and four siblings underwent testing to determine whether any of them could be a suitable donor for a bone marrow transplant.A transplant can replace damaged or failing blood-forming cells with healthy stem cells from a compatible donor. For patients with severe aplastic anemia, a stem cell or bone marrow transplant can potentially provide a curative treatment, particularly when a suitable donor is available.For Emma’s family, the search eventually produced extraordinary news: her 2-year-old sister, Lucy, was identified as a perfect match.According to an exclusive report by PEOPLE, Lucy was able to donate bone marrow to her older sister, allowing Emma to undergo the transplant on February 17, 2026. Before the procedure, Emma received chemotherapy as part of the transplant process. Lucy, meanwhile, was described by her mother as being brave throughout the donation process.The transplant went well, and Emma and her mother returned home to Pleasant Grove in March, according to PEOPLE. By late May, Emma had reached the 100-day milestone following the transplant without complications and celebrated her fifth birthday by ringing the bell at the children's hospital.Although the transplant marked an important milestone, Emma's recovery has continued. PEOPLE reported that she remained immunocompromised and continued to require medical care and precautions after returning home.Her family has also relied on community support throughout the ordeal. The GoFundMe fundraiser was created to help cover medical expenses associated with Emma’s hospital care, testing, chemotherapy and bone marrow transplant.The fundraiser reflects how quickly Emma’s illness transformed everyday family life. Her mother wrote that the long hospital stays and numerous medical tests had created significant financial pressure, while also thanking friends, relatives and community members for supporting the family.For Emma and Lucy, the experience has created a bond that goes beyond being sisters. Lucy’s donation gave Emma a chance to recover from a life-threatening illness and return home to her family.Amanda told PEOPLE, Emma has become increasingly aware that Lucy helped save her life. The two sisters have developed a particularly strong connection since the transplant, with Emma often looking out for her younger sister.Emma's story began with a frightening diagnosis just days before Christmas. About two months later, the discovery that her toddler sister was a perfect donor match offered the family a path forward, turning an extraordinarily difficult chapter into one marked by hope, recovery and an enduring bond between two sisters.
Article Summary: Emma Meline was diagnosed with severe aplastic anemia just days before Christmas 2025. Two months later, the family learned that her 2-year-old sister was a perfect bone marrow match. Lucy was able to donate bone marrow to her older sister, allowing Emma to undergo the transplant on February 17, 2026. The transplant went well, and Emma and her mother returned home in March.

Article Title: Indian man on death row in the US for killing wife, in-laws in 2019 seeks retrial, says his previous lawyers were bad
Article Text:
Indian man Gurpreet Singh, who is on death row for killing wife and in-laws, is seeking fresh trial in Ohio.

Gurpreet Singh's secret affair

In 2019, Gurpreet Singh, an Indian-origin truck driver in Ohio, called 911 and reported that his wife and her family had been killed. When cops arrived, they found four bodies, all shot to death, and Singh had blood splatters and gunshot residue on his body. Singh was not arrested immediately but after three months.Ohio had a halt on the death penalty in 2020 as Gov Mike DeWine then said that there were not enough lethal injection drugs available.In 2024, death penalty returned as Singh was given a death sentence for killing four people: his wife Shalinderjit Kaur, 39; her parents Parmjit Kaur, 62, and Hakiakat Singh Pannag, 59 and his wife’s aunt, Amarjit Kaur, 58. The date of Singh's execution was set for November 27 that year, but Singh appealed for a retrial.After two trials on taxpayers' money, Singh is now seeking a third trial.Earlier this week, Kathryn Sandford asked the Ohio Supreme Court for another fresh trial, calling the previous attorneys ineffective. Sandford said Gurpreet's first language is Punjabi and hence there might have been a language barrier.Taxpayers paid $180,206.26 for Singh’s defense at both trials, according to Butler County Common Pleas Court Administrator Wayne Gilkison in 2024.The judge declared him indigent before the first trial and Singh retained his private attorneys who were hired and paid for by his family, but the county had to pay for additional expenses such as defense experts and four interpreters. Butler County Prosecutor Mike Gmoser said his office spent another $26,552.61 to prosecute, including travel to locate and interview experts and witnesses.At the time of his wife’s killing, Gurpreet Singh had been living a double life. His attorneys conceded in documents that he had been having an affair with another woman and had purchased a home near her nine months before the murders. Prosecutors said that Gurpreet Singh killed his family because he could no longer support both his mistress and his wife’s household on his salary as a truck driver.No other shooter's name came up in the investigation.

Article Title: Teen dressed as clown stabs 78-year-old man to death near St. Louis bus stop
Article Text: A 15-year-old boy has been charged with first-degree murder after a 78-year-old man was found stabbed to death near a bus stop in the St Louis area in what police described as a random attack, AP reported.Investigators said video footage shows the suspect wearing a clown costume around the time of the killing.The victim was identified as John W. Allen, who was found on a street in East St Louis, Illinois, on Monday. He was pronounced dead at the scene.Illinois State Police said they reviewed video evidence showing the teenager dressed in a clown costume near the time of the incident. Authorities have not released details on where the footage came from or what it shows beyond the suspect’s appearance.Officers arrested the teenager at a residence in East St Louis after identifying him as a suspect.
